python -c "
text = '''I built an open-source safety layer for AI coding agents. Here is why, how it works, and what broke along the way.

The problem

Autonomous AI coding agents like Antigravity can run commands on your machine: inspect repositories, edit files, and run terminal scripts. By default, they ask permission for every single action.

That gets exhausting fast. After dozens of confirmation prompts for harmless commands like git status, you start clicking yes without reading. Or you flip on auto-accept, and now nothing gets checked at allâ€”including the one destructive command that could wipe your files or push breaking changes.

It is all or nothing. I wanted something in between.

What I built

It is called Agent Airlock. It intercepts tool calls at the agent lifecycle boundary before they reach your operating system.

- Obvious cases get decided instantly by fixed rules. Safe read-only commands go straight through. Destructive commands like recursive root deletions are blocked outright. No model is involved, and it resolves in under a millisecond.
- Ambiguous commands, like a force-push or unfamiliar script, go to a small model running locally on my laptop (ModernBERT via Laya). It estimates blast radius and reversibility to decide whether to allow, block, or ask.
- A circuit breaker watches for autoregressive failure loops. If the agent keeps retrying an identical failing fix, the airlock steps in and halts the loop.
- If anything goes wrongâ€”like the daemon timing out or the model being uncertainâ€”it strictly defaults to human confirmation. It never silently fails open.

What broke along the way

This was the most informative part of the project:

1. The base model labeled everything safe. Out of the box, stock Laya labeled all 15 of my test commands \"safe\", including rm -rf / and curl-to-shell. I had to build a fine-tuning pipeline on 200 labeled developer operations across 21 tool families to fix routing and calibrate temperatures.
2. The model was 92% confident kill -9 was safe. It was not broken; my training data labeled single-PID kills as safe, while my test rubric expected human review. The model had simply learned my label. A model is only as sound as its labeling heuristics.
3. The timing illusion. I initially saw sub-millisecond model timings before realizing I was measuring asynchronous CPU dispatch without waiting for the GPU stream to finish. The real warm GPU inference is around 38ms.
4. A wrapper broke the circuit breaker. In my first benchmark, the circuit breaker missed a 4-attempt failure loop because each retry printed a different attempt banner, altering the hash. I had to add prefix wrapper stripping so cosmetic text does not defeat loop detection.

Honest limits

This was evaluated on a single scripted comparison, not a statistically averaged benchmark across many trials. More importantly, the training labels, safe thresholds, and benchmark tasks reflect my personal threat model and risk tolerance. This is not an ISO or SOC2 certified safety authority, and it should not be treated as a universal standard.

The entire dataset, training script, and codebase are open source (Apache 2.0) so you can review label boundaries and retrain it for your own environment.

Please refer to the attached technical whitepaper for the full architecture breakdown, validation curves, and benchmark logs.

Repo: github.com/dev_user/agent-airlock
Weights: huggingface.co/ruddh/agent-airlock-laya'''

print('Word count:', len(text.split()))
"

# .jev-policy.yaml â€” Workspace Policy Configuration for Jev Airlock
# Place this file in the root of your workspace/repository to tailor rules
# to your project's build system, scripts, and workflows.

version: "1.0"

# Disallow project-level rules from overriding bundled hard-deny rules
# (Setting this to true requires conscious security approval)
allow_override_denies: false

# Custom project rules
rules:
  # Example 1: Hard-allow harmless project-specific build or lint scripts
  - rule_id: "allow-project-build"
    tool_name: "run_command"
    pattern: '^npm (run (build|lint|test|typecheck)|test)$'
    action: "allow"
    description: "Allow standard workspace npm scripts without prompt"

  - rule_id: "allow-python-pytest"
    tool_name: "run_command"
    pattern: '^(pytest|python -m pytest)( [a-zA-Z0-9_\-\./]+)*$'
    action: "allow"
    description: "Allow project unit tests execution"

  # Example 2: Hard-deny access to local database or private credential files
  - rule_id: "deny-sqlite-database-tampering"
    tool_name: "run_command"
    pattern: 'rm .*(\.sqlite|\.db|\.sqlite3)$'
    action: "deny"
    description: "Block deletion of local database files"

  - rule_id: "deny-read-local-service-keys"
    tool_name: "view_file"
    pattern: '.*(secrets\.json|service-account\.json)$'
    action: "deny"
    description: "Block model inspection of local secrets and service keys"
